posts.hook: Two apparel campaigns. One got 1,318 leads. The other got 19. If you only looked at the count, you'd think the first one won.
posts.body:
Two apparel campaigns. One got 1,318 leads. The other got 19.

If you only looked at the count, you'd think the first one won.

1,318 was a domestic knitwear campaign, ₹19 a lead. Cheap, fast, the form open to anyone who wanted to fill it.

19 was a UK wholesale campaign for apparel buyers. The ad form said it upfront: 200-piece minimum order. Under $6 an enquiry, and every single one was a buyer who could actually place that order.

The form did the filtering before the sales team had to.

Most people building a lead form think their job is to get the number up. It isn't. Your job is to make the wrong person leave before they click submit.

If you sell in bulk, put the minimum quantity in the ad or the form itself. If you have a price floor, say it. You will lose volume. You will stop wasting time on leads that were never going to convert.

Nova Attire, a Tirupur manufacturer, generated 4,248 wholesale buyer leads at ₹16.58 each across six campaigns over the ten months we ran their account. Even there, we never captured how many became actual orders — nothing sent that outcome back to Meta. That's a gap I'd fix differently now: qualify harder in the form, and always track the sale, not just the lead.

If you want a second pair of eyes on your own lead form, I open up free audits some weeks — happy to look at yours.

#leadgeneration #metaads #tirupur

UNVERIFIED: "every single one was a buyer who could actually place that order" — No approved fact confirms that all 19 UK leads were verified as able to place a 200-piece order; this is an inferred outcome, not a documented fact.

UNVERIFIED: "Only buyers who could actually order 200 pieces bothered to fill it in." — States as fact that only qualified buyers filled the form; this is an inferred outcome not confirmed by any approved data (conversion/order data was never captured for Nova Attire, and no such verification exists for the UK campaign either).
UNVERIFIED: "Every one already qualified before the first call." — Asserts pre-qualification of all 19 leads as fact; no approved data supports this outcome.

check: "Get this wrong and you pay a sales team to chase people who were never buying." — Implies a specific client consequence (paying a sales team to chase unqualified leads) not established by any approved fact.

slides.text: Get this wrong and you pay a sales team to chase people who were never buying.
Campaign one: domestic knitwear leads. Anyone could fill the form. ₹19 each.
1,318 people said yes to a knitwear ad. Nobody asked how much they wanted to buy.
Campaign two: UK wholesale apparel buyers. The form said 200-piece minimum order, upfront.
Only buyers who could actually order 200 pieces bothered to fill it in.
Result: 19 leads. Under $6 an enquiry. Every one already qualified before the first call.
Same product category. Same platform. One number 69 times bigger than the other.
The bigger number wasn't the win. The form that filtered people out was.
1,318 wide leads vs 19 narrow ones — the form decides which one you get.
Put your minimum order, your price floor, your real requirement inside the form itself.
A smaller number of the right people beats a bigger number of the wrong ones.
